subtopic: NORTH SASKATCHEWAN
NORTH SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Has the Minister of National Health and Welfare any further information on the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river?

subtopic: NORTH SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I should like to outline in some detail the present situation, the steps which have been taken and the proposals which are made for future action.
Before doing so however 1 am sure that the house will be glad to learn that a number of the substances in the water have been identified, and certain of these are thought by the investigators to be involved in the source of the trouble.
As a result of these findings, recommendations were made to the health authorities of the province, and the members will have already been advised by the press and the radio of the action taken by the provincial department of health in issuing instructions to one of the companies suspected of discharging wastes containing these substances, to discontinue by March 1 the discharge of such wastes into the North Saskatchewan river. It is understood that appropriate steps are being taken to pond or isolate such wastes for subsequent disposition.
It is very much hoped that this action will prove effective in bringing about some alleviation of the distress of the communities which are dependent upon the river for their domestic water supplies.
I can assure the house that my department will continue to assist in every way that it can, to co-operate with provincial authorities and with industry to seek a final solution of the problem, and to give such advice and help as it can to avoid any recurrence, once a solution is found. It may meanwhile be of interest to recapitulate briefly the events which have led up to the present situation and the efforts which have been made at the federal level to assist provincial authorities.
Questions
I have from time to time reported to the house on the developments as they have taken place, and it may be useful at this time to say something of the specific plans formulated in co-operation with provincial authorities which are presently being implemented by the technical officers, both at the federal and the provincial level.
While the problem was thought to have resulted from the discharge of industrial wastes into the river at or near the city of Edmonton, the solution to this problem was complicated by a number of factors which include climatic and geographical conditions, as well as the diversity of wastes which are being discharged into the river by a number of industries.
The identification, therefore, of the particular offending substance, as well as of the particular industry responsible for its discharge into the river, represented a scientific project of some magnitude. I think I should say that diligent inquiries were made from all possible sources in Canada, as well as in the United States where similar problems might have been encountered, but it appeared that this particular situation was without exact precedent in any of the communities in North America.
The considered opinion of the Scientific? investigators, at the federal and provincial! and the industry level, was that while an immediate solution was of course the urgent objective to be found, the over-all problem of providing safe but effective means of disposal of industrial wastes made it necessary to obtain a precise chemical answer, and this could only be found through the laborious but nevertheless necessary field work, sampling, analyses and other procedures, whereby the identification of the substance or substances and methods for treatment could be devised.
I emphasize these features because it might otherwise have appeared that the shut-down of all of the industries which could have been involved would provide the answer. This however would not be the case, as it is only through investigation of the river in its present condition that a permanent solution to the problem could be expected.
With the investigations that were made and the information that was available, it was obvious that the problem was accordingly one of great complexity, and it seemed to us that the solution would likely be found only with the full utilization of all available technical resources.
As I previously advised the house, I therefore communicated with the minister of health of Alberta, under date of February 8,

Questions
offering full co-operation and assistance of the technical officers of the department to participate in a joint study with the provincial authorities and with industries, in seeking an immediate solution with the further objective of making recommendations which would result in an over-all solution to the problem of treating such wastes in that area.
This offer was accepted by the minister of health of Alberta, and immediately technical officers of the department left for Edmonton to work out, in co-operation with provincial and industry officers, procedures which might offer the most expeditious solution.
After an intensive study of the area of industrial development downstream from Edmonton by officers from the occupational health and public health engineering divisions of this department, in company with provincial experts as well as experts from industry, certain procedures were evolved.
The objective of the study as was conceived by the federal representatives was twofold:
1.	To eliminate the offensive taste and odour from the waters of the North Saskatchewan river.
2.	To carry out a comprehensive investigation of industrial pollution to establish the basis for future control.
It was emphasized that every effort must be made to provide as quickly as possible, a solution for objective No. 1, and if a solution could not readily be found, it would be necessary to recommend drastic action.
The detailed steps which were recommended involved the following:
It was recommended that for purposes of industrial appraisal, arrangements be made to have two investigating teams set up to carry out a rapid but detailed study of the industries. Each team would be composed of an industrial hygienist and public health engineer from federal resources. These federal experts would work closely with experts in industry, the provincial government, the national and the Alberta research councils and the university authorities.
A member of this group would be responsible for the over-all co-ordination of this phase of the study.
In addition to the industrial appraisal, sampling procedures would be developed as rapidly as possible to include analyses of industrial effluents and river water. The sampling process would extend from a point above Edmonton to the various centres complaining of pollution in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, thus covering many hundreds of miles.

A third proposal involved analytical investigations to include all possible methods of analysis to determine the nature of the pollutant, as well as intensive investigation of any leads that might indicate its possible nature. It was hoped from the analytical investigations to provide leads as to the nature of the offending substance and thus to achieve objective No. 1 as rapidly as possible.
By way of illustration, one lead has been developed and is being followed at the present time. It was found that a synthetic mixture of propanol and butanol in water produced a material with an odour similar to the odour of the water samples taken from the river at points downstream from the industrial development.
A fourth phase of the investigation involved the extraction of materials from plant effluents which are known to or which might cause offence. This would be developed as part of the industrial appraisal during which time every effort would be made to have the companies remove materials that are known to or which might cause offence from their effluents.
As soon as substances causing the taste and odour nuisance have been identified, suitable procedures would of course be followed for the diversion and disposal of these materials.
The above were the specific steps which the federal officers suggested as constituting the most suitable, but at the same time, expeditious method of proceeding to study the problem and to obtain some alleviation from present distress for the affected communities.
In order to carry out these procedures and to reach the desired objectives as quickly as possible, it was emphasized that a co-ordinated and all-out approach must be adopted. The industries agreed to co-operate actively in the investigation and to make available all technical resources which they possessed. It was also thought desirable that other resources within the province, such as the Alberta research council and the facilities of the university, should be utilized as well as the assistance of the regional laboratory of the national research council at the city of Saskatoon.
In addition the environmental health centre in Cincinnati were asked to assist and their efforts will complement other aspects of the investigation.
The work which was immediately undertaken in accordance with these plans is presently proceeding and, as I mentioned at the outset of this statement, as a result a number of substances have positively been

recognized and identified in the water at Prince Albert and certain of these substances may be the ones contributing to the difficulty.
In addition to the specific action which was proposed, I thought it desirable to communicate with the minister of health respecting the measures his government proposed to initiate to rectify the present situation, as well as those involving the general problem of the overloading of the North Saskatchewan river by the discharge of industrial and other wastes.
Under date of February 22, I received from the minister of health a reply to my telegram, in which he outlined the steps which his government had originally taken to prevent the development of this situation and he indicated the progress being made through the technical assistance which had been given and of his hope for an early solution.
He moreover advised that, in default of an immediate solution, the provincial authorities would be prepared to take steps to see that all suspected wastes were diverted into a pond or ravine for subsequent disposal, when this could be done without danger of a recurrence of the present situation.
Action has accordingly been taken in this connection as was announced by the authorities of the province of Alberta on February 25.
I am sure that the house will recognize that the problem is one of great complexity, that its solution is not a simple one, and that the federal government has done everything possible to assist in finding a solution.
The government will continue to assist the responsible authorities in every way that it can, through the provision of technical personnel and facilities, until a solution is found and measures can be adopted which will provide some satisfactory basis for control to avoid further pollution of the waters and consequent distress to the communities that are dependent upon it.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Green.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the beginning of the sixth day of this debate. I think if there had been a proper sense of urgency on the part of the government as to the importance of this debate it would not have lasted for even six minutes; because I see no reason whatsoever why the government should not have accepted the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I
2528	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment think the only reason is that the government, in its, shall I say, arrogance, does not like to admit that any wisdom or knowledge can come from any quarter in the house except from themselves.
The attitude throughout has been, "Father knows best; leave everything to us". I want to read from the amendment to show exactly what it asks. It did not ask for any panic action. It did not suggest that it knew the answer. What it said was this:
. . . that a select committee should be appointed immediately for the purpose of examining into and reporting upon the actual unemployment situation throughout Canada and for the purpose of making recommendations to this house as to short-term and long-term methods for dealing effectively with this problem.
As I say, no blue ruin attitude was taken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra; there was no suggestion about any "catastrophe" or any "chaos". It was a sensible suggestion that this thing should be looked into. And what have we got from the government? We have nothing but "Wait and see". I say that it did not seem to have any sense of urgency whatever; but I do suggest that there is a feeling of urgency and of great urgency on the part of those who are unemployed. They will find no counterpart to that attitude here; and I feel sure that those people would think it reasonable to examine into and report upon the actual unemployment situation.
Certainly it is not because the facts are clear that nothing needs to be inquired into. The labour people have suggested-they have stated-that there are more than 500,000 unemployed; but from the government we have nothing but a babble of voices. The figures used by the different ministers have differed, not merely by thousands, not merely even by tens of thousands, but by hundreds of thousands. We have seen what could be described as "confusion worse confounded". The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Acting Prime Minister, was frank in the remarks he made about unemployment to the textile and agricultural implement workers. But when we come to the actual figures used by the ministers, as I say, we find confusion. There must be scores of economists in the various departments who prepare those figures; but one can only assume, because we believe they are competent men, that the government has so bedevilled the situation with a variety of views and a variety of approaches to the facts that, as I say, all kinds of figures are given to us.
Again I ask, what is the objection to this inquiry? No sensible objection that I have
tMr. Macdonnell.]

heard has been raised. On the face of it, it seems sensible. The government in effect say, "Let the situation develop; let us have time". Well, there is a standing committee available, and why on earth should it not be allowed to tackle this problem? No; to allow a committee would apparently involve a most damaging admission. It would involve the admission that the government is not omniscient, and that possible useful suggestions could arise from elsewhere. The reasoning apparently goes like this.
The government is omniscient.
To create a committee would be to admit that the government is not omniscient.
Therefore we must not have a committee.
I want to emphasize the fact that the resolution was moved in moderate terms, and that the words "doom" and "gloom", which I see they use in the United States, have not been used in our debate. I now want to look in more detail at the various complicated figures which we got from various members of the government. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), whose appetite for facts is keener than that of some of the other ministers who spoke, gave us these figures of January 23, at page 2085 of Hansard:
It is estimated that at January 23, 357,000 people worked fewer than 35 hours; another 139,000 had jobs but did no work during the survey week, owing to temporary lay-offs, illness, labour disputes, bad weather and a number of other miscellaneous reasons; while there were 280,000 persons who were, to quote the phrase of the dominion bureau of statistics, "without jobs and seeking work".
Now, the minister gave us those figures but did not seem to have very much to say as to what was to follow from them. He did not think the time had come for an excursion into public works. He suggested that fiscal and monetary policies, which would come from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), might deal with the situation, and accordingly we asked the Minister of Finance what he had to say about it, and at page 2026 of Hansard the minister said in part:
If economic activity declines, the government is in a position to take stronger action in these and other directions, but I should like to emphasize that as I and my colleagues view the present situation there is no justification for stronger action and I have a high degree of confidence that when our winter season of normally reduced activity is passed, economic activity in Canada is likely to resume its upward trend at a satisfactory rate.
Well, there is not much sense of urgency there, Mr. Speaker. We also have a reference from the Minister of Finance in an interview that he had with some of the labour

people. It is reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 12, and here are the minister's words in quotation marks:
"While we should not bury our heads in the sand and say everything is fine", Mr. Abbott declared, "we should be careful and not paint too gloomy a picture, because I do not think it is justified."
"The plans of people with regard to business can be affected by too much talk of rising unemployment and a possible recession". "I think we should be a little careful about taking too gloomy a view about the prospects."
T.L.C. president Bengough said: "I think there are 580,000 out of work. The situation is serious."
Mr. Abbott replied: "I would not say the situation is serious. I would say it is unpleasant. There certainly is higher unemployment than we would like to see."
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that he was certainly not taking it too seriously; indeed his cheerful attitude almost reminded us of the minister on budget night announcing a large unexpected surplus and referring to "buoyant" revenues.
Now we come to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and I wish to read some comments which he made on the situation because he outlined it in what I think were very sensible terms. The minister described the business situation in what I think were well considered terms. He said, as reported at page 2104 of Hansard:
Toward the latter part of 1953 those indicators which gauged the over-all level of activity in the economy began to level off, and in a few cases have declined slightly. This change in trend reflects largely a reduction in the pressure of demand rather than any decline in over-all volume. In other words requirements, which in the past two or three years have been mounting rapidly, are now simply not expanding at the same rate. This applies to expenditures for defence and for other government requirements, . . .
And later on I read:
This levelling off in demand, taken in conjunction with the moderate decline in activity in the United States' economy, has brought a change in the tempo of business activity in Canada. This type of situation is invariably accompanied by a hesitancy on the part of business in placing orders, more hand-to-mouth buying, and a tendency to reduce inventories. This causes a temporary slow-down in the pace of business which in the present instance has coincided with the seasonally slack period in the economy.
And finally:
Such a situation admittedly gives rise to a good deal of anxiety and. I think, has been prematurely interpreted by many as the beginning of a recessionary trend.
Now, having used these words of moderation and warning, the minister rollicked off to tell us about the billions which he so loves to speak about, and of course billions are important.
His equanimity was considerably assisted by using figures that were very much below those of the Minister of Labour. The only figure which agreed with those of the Minister of Labour was 280,000 "without jobs
Proposed Committee on Unemployment and seeking work". Instead of 357,000 people who, according to the Minister of Labour, "worked fewer than 35 hours", we heard from the Acting Prime Minister that 65,000 persons were "on short time", or were "laid off for part of the week". Instead of 139,000 who, according to the Minister of Labour, "had jobs but did no work during the survey week", the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned 24,000 who "for the full week in question were temporarily laid off".
Moreover, after drastically reducing the numbers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that they should not be added up. The minister is much better at subtraction than he is at addition, apparently. For the rest of his speech the minister found it convenient to refer to the 280,000, ignoring those who had worked fewer than 35 hours a week and also those who during the week of the inquiry were out of work. I suggest that it makes an awful lot of difference whether a man is working 34 hours and 59 minutes or 20 hours, or whether he is working 15 hours or 5 hours, but apparently those considerations were ignored.
Now, the minister's carelessness in that, may have been partly due to an explanation that he gave us in regard to the figure of unemployed. He told us about some of those on the list who apparently, as far as 1 can make out from the explanation of the minister, just put their names down, as you might say, just for the hell of it, or not very seriously.
I think we could call this a real star turn and I should think that it would be of great encouragement to all the poor fellows who are out of work. The reference is to people who go on the lists for special reasons, and particularly to the woods workers in the minister's area. He said, and I quote from page 2106 of Hansard of February 15:
When the cutting is finished the rr.cn return to town, and most of them go back to the little farms they have in the vicinity of Port Arthur. Before doing so, however, they stop at the employment office, register as unemployed, and request their unemployment benefits. It is quite proper that they should do so. Then when the drive comes on in the early spring, when the rivers start to open, they return to the forest and take care of the hauling and driving of the timber down the river.
And again:
That has been their program, and it has been going on for a good many years.
In that way, apparently the minister comforts himself. He then comes to the bedtime story of the man we might refer to as the rich unemployed, and I quote again from page 2106:
I recall an incident that occurred when I was there about a year ago. A man I knew from my construction days approached me and said that he
2530	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment had just arrived in town from a lumber camp. He wanted to know if I knew where he could get a job. I said, "Do you really want a job?" He said, "I will take a job." I said, "Have you registered for unemployment insurance?" He said, "No; do you think I would stand in line for $24 a week?" That was his attitude. I said, "How much money have you in your pocket?" I will not name the sum, but it was such as to lead me to believe that he was not very anxious to get employment. That situation applies in many parts of Canada. It applies to a good many jobs that are seasonal and always have been seasonal.
I am sure that that gave comfort to the minister and I suppose it will give comfort to the unemployed. I suggest to the minister that he have that part of his speech printed and sent to all the unemployed. I think it would offer great encouragement to them and stimulate them perhaps to get into the same class themselves.
While I am dealing with the question of figures I will refer to the remarks of the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey). He solved the problem of the figures even more easily than the minister because he ignored all except the 280,000. He had no interest in the 357,000 who are working less than 35 hours a week and the 139,000 who apparently are out of work. His conclusions are very simple and entirely in line with my suggestion. He really just told the rest of us to be good little boys and leave everything to the government and everything will be well.
I quote what the hon. member said as reported on page 2177 of Hansard of February 17:
AH I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that it is my impression that few people have learned the lessons of their experience and know better how to apply them than the Acting Prime Minister in this house.
I should not omit to say that a little earlier in his speech he referred also to the Acting Prime Minister and to an address which he had made some years ago at Dalhousie University. I think it would be suitable also to refer to the eulogy which came also from the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). The hon. member for Fort William does not like to let the sun set without having said something eulogistic about the Acting Prime Minister. That is very nice too, and I do not see why anyone should object. I continue reading from what the hon. member for Halifax said:
I can assure the hon. member that it does not require his suggestion to have the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his colleagues apply to the solution of this problem and the other serious problems that from time to time face the people of Canada and the government of Canada the experiences and the knowledge and the abilities that they have found from their long and useful life in this country in many fields, and not the least their contribution to the public life of this country as members of the government.
I am sure that the minister welcomed what he had to say. As I listened to the debate;
[M. Macdonnell.l

as I listened to the way the numbers of unemployed were being whittled down, 10,000 here, 100,000 there; as I listened to the rising tide of eulogies on the government, and particularly on the Acting Prime Minister; it seemed to me that as I looked the unemployed faded away more and more into the distance and the figure of the Acting Prime Minister rose almost with a halo around it. It occurred to me that the title of the debate might be, "To the glory of Howe and in memory of the unemployed."

speechtext: Carefully thought out.

speechtext:
I am sure the minister would not expect me to be unfair in any way, and it would be very unfair not to point out that he did make a constructive suggestion. It is to that that I wish now to refer. I think it is an original suggestion.
Far be it from me to set myself up as an economist, but I have often talked to economists and near-economists. The suggestion, to be found on page 2106 of Hansard, has the merit of originality and perhaps may have some effect upon the speech to which we will be listening in some weeks by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It seems to suggest that there is a very simple way to deal with the unemployed, and that is to keep taxes higher and higher. I quote from page 2106 as follows:
We have been reminded that our government expenditures are high. Again they are high because the government foresaw that this would be a difficult year.
It is all there, you see, Mr. Speaker. Everything is foreseen. It is wonderful, really.
The transition from a seller's market to a buyer's market is always difficult. Certainly the worst way in which to meet a transition of that kind is to curtail government investment. That is the old theory that did not work so well back in 1931, that when things get tough the government should stop spending and start squeezing its pocketbook.
I was surprised at comparing 1954 with 1931. I thought hon. members opposite had always thought that such a comparison should not be made.
That is not the time to cut government spending. There were important investments that the government needed to make and, in the light of the general situation, it was decided that this would be a year to loosen the purse strings and step up our public works program, now that military construction is less active. That has been the policy of the government for 1954.
As I say, I had thought that if there was one thing on which there was widespread agreement it was that when there is a business slackening off the best way to stimulate or ginger it up is to reduce taxes. I thought that that was almost universally agreed. I am not overlooking the fact that the minister

used the word "investment". I am not suggesting that there is no such thing as sound government investment, but the words that are used seem to me to introduce the most extreme fallacy at a time when we are being warned on all sides that we are becoming a high-cost economy. I should like to quote briefly from one or two statements to show that the minister's view is, I think, not widely held. At the annual meeting of the Royal Bank of Canada the president had this to say:
I felt obliged last year to voice some doubts about the permanence of a prosperity built so largely on the "treacherous sands of consumer credit."
Everybody wishes to avoid the evils of recession and at the same time to avoid the risk of further inflation. It seems clear therefore that we must depend more largely on the other two methods of stimulating and sustaining demand, namely, tax reductions and price reductions.
Then there is a voice from the United States. The New York Times recently said:
The administration had two powerful antirecession weapons at its disposal, easy money and tax reduction incentives. Few will disagree either in Wall street or Main street that tax reduction probably would be the more effective at this junction.
Without entirely dismissing the idea of government investment, surely if one thing is clear beyond others it is that taxes put up costs and impede exports. There is an interesting comment on this in an article by E. C. Ertl in the current Financial Times as follows:
We have wilfully, or through default of leadership, given in to every pressure that was leading to higher costs.
And again:
We have, in fact, insisted that the foreign buyer whose need for our products was great indeed, would subsidize our high standard of living, by charging him prices he could afford to pay just that long.
To the extent to which his productive capacity has grown again, to that extent does he now refuse to buy from us.
Those are serious words which we should all ponder. It has been demonstrated in this house again and again that taxes do and indeed must put up costs. When we anxiously consider our foreign trade I rather think it will astonish the great bulk of thoughtful people in the business world that the minister should state the reason for which high taxes will remain. But I think we can all imagine that there is one place where the news will be good and where it will be well received. Can you not imagine, Mr. Speaker, when the various departments- which the Minister of Finance assures us and, I am sure, sincerely, that he is trying to keep down to the lowest penny-read these words, the joy with which they will be received. The Acting Prime Minister said, "The worst way in which to meet a transition is to curtail
Proposed Committee on Unemployment government investment" and, further down, "it was decided that this would be a year to loosen the purse strings".
I can imagine that those words would be received with great enthusiasm throughout all the departments and that the news would percolate like a great fructifying flood to all the people whose requests have been turned down by the Minister of Finance. What a fortunate thing it is for all these people that the supplementary estimates are still available. At any rate, it is nice to think that there will be some people who will be in favour of what the minister says. Incidentally, when we remember that in spite of the lowering of defence expenditures our over-all expenditures are up, we can assume that that attitude has already had its effect throughout the departments.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, while as I have argued there is no sense of urgency here, events outside are not standing still. There are disquieting reports, which we get in increasing numbers, of Canadian industries that are feeling the pinch here and there; of Canadian companies, controlled in the United States, which are being by-passed by the parent company which can sell its product cheaper in Canada than can the Canadian subsidiary of American companies which are excluding Canadian subsidiaries from the export trade.
As the minister said in his words that I read a while ago, it is a situation which gives rise to a good deal of anxiety. Of course, the fact that there is great anxiety in the United States undoubtedly adds to that feeling. This is the 1st of March. We are beginning a month which is supposed to be the deadline month in the United States. The President has told them that if things were not improving by March, the government would have to step in with more vigorous action.
One of the troubles is that we get optimistic opinions from two quarters that do not amount to much-of course I am referring now to people outside of this house-one group who speak out of the fulness of their ignorance, and others who are well informed but who nevertheless feel that they must not use any but optimistic words lest they actually worsen the situation. Our socialist brethren have offered us their old nostrums. I can only suggest to them that if they will study what is going on in England I think they will find that their English colleagues have turned up their noses already at some of the cure-alls that they were worshipping years ago.
I come back to our resolution, and I stress again the moderation of its terms. I suggest that it would be the most natural thing in the world to adopt it because what the government is saying is this, and 1 do not criticize
2532	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment them for saying it. They are saying, "Wait and see". That can go a little longer; not much longer but a little bit longer. What on earth would be more natural in that period of waiting and seeing than to do what this resolution calls for? I stress again that the resolution is in moderate terms. It merely suggests in effect that two heads are better than one or that three or four heads are better than one.
Any man of common sense knows that a great deal of inquiry is necessary. The only question is whether the government should make it a party matter, and no reason that appeals to me has been given for that procedure. I shall therefore vote for the amendment.

But when the hon. member came to make practical suggestions as to what might be done about unemployment, he seemed to have just one and that was a reduction in taxes. I suggest that is the kind of suggestion that would get almost unanimous support from the people of Canada.

I am not making a speech for the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre or for the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I am not making one either for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I will endeavour to make my own. I say that the idea of tax reduction may be something that would have almost unanimous support across the country. But before I myself went along with the suggestion now made that taxes should be reduced in the coming budget, I would ask "Whose taxes?" If it is a reduction of taxes of big business, if it is a repetition of reduction in taxes on the wealthy, as we had in last year's budget, then I would not be in favour of such a tax reduction. If it was a reduction in taxes for the mass of the Canadian people who will go out and spend the extra income they receive through a reduction in taxes, then of course I should support such a reduction.
IMr. Macdonnell.]

The hon. member for Greenwood quoted another statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Speaking in this debate, as reported at page 2106 of Hansard, the minister said:
... it was decided that this would be a year to loosen the purse strings and step up our public works program, now that military construction is less active.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said, "This is a year to loosen the purse strings". That is all he said. He did not say how the purse strings were going to be loosened. He did not say in what way government expenditures would be stepped up. The most disturbing thing that has come out of this debate, to my mind, is not really whether one set of figures about the number of unemployed is correct or whether another set of figures is correct but the fact that, as the debate has gone on, it has become more and more clear that the government has no policy with which to deal with unemployment. If unemployment should correct itself when spring comes, it is just good luck as far as the government is concerned. But if unemployment should continue-as there is every sign it will-then the government has not yet told parliament and the people of Canada what it would do as a government to alleviate such unemployment. Back in 1945 after the war a white paper was issued by the government. In it the government set forth the proposals it was making to deal with any possible unemployment that might arise. There was to be a large shelf of public works and as unemployment appeared some of those public works were to be taken off the shelf and be put into operation. This debate has continued for two full weeks and we have heard nothing of the shelf of projects to deal with unemployment that was talked of in 1945. Apparently the idea of this government proceeding with public works on a vast scale as a method of dealing with unemployment and correcting unemployment has long been abandoned.

speechtext:
Canada has supported a plan for the trans-Canada highway, but I suggest that the government, now that unemployment has reached a total of 500,000, should consider assisting the municipalities by providing grants for the building of market roads. If the government would undertake such grants, I am sure that municipalities generally across this dominion would be prepared to use those grants and thus help correct the severe unemployment problem that is with us now.
Some people have always said, well it is all right to advocate spending money but where are you going to get all the money that is necessary for such a proposal? I say it is not a question of how much money it will cost; it is not a question basically of where we shall get the money. The question is this: Does Canada now have resources that are not being fully utilized? I say the answer is yes, we have a half a million unemployed and we have all the basic raw materials that are necessary for an adequate road and highway system. I suggest that the time has now come when our federal government should be giving greater leadership and more financial assistance to the building of roads. A system of road grants should be inaugurated to enable municipalities to undertake an adequate system of roads. If such were now undertaken in Canada we would be just forty years behind the United States in starting such a road program.
I believe the government should consider also the proposition that has been frequently advanced in this house by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), namely, that there should be federal grants for education. In the brief presented by the UAW-CIO- CCL, it is stated that Canada needs thousands of elementary school classrooms. The brief points out that with Canada's rapidly growing population we now have 63 per cent more children of public school age than we had some ten years ago. I believe the federal government should promote the construction of adequate schools as a further means of dealing with the serious unemployment problem we now have.
For years now I have advocated the expansion of one field of social security, namely, an increase in the family allowances. If family allowances in Canada were increased, there would be an immediate increased demand for Canadian textiles and food, both of which are in surplus supply now. And further, I should like to see the government adopt an adequate and farsighted program to assist agriculture. In advocating such a program I do not think I could put the need for

such a program more clearly than it is set forth in the brief presented by the UAW. On page 10, it says:
The impressive and productive efforts of Canadian farmers to assure Canada abundance of food and fibre should not be rewarded by depressing the living standards of the people who work the land.
A full employment program must assure full equity to the farmer in exchanging the things he grows for the things he buys, and include national policies to restore the overseas markets that Canadian farmers have lost since the end of world war II. The 1929 depression proved beyond doubt that the prosperity of industrial workers and the prosperity of farmers are inseparably tied together. Canadian farmers need more tractors, trucks, combines and other agricultural implements which our agricultural implement industry is capable of producing, but our farmers either cannot afford or are not now buying this equipment because of their fear and uncertainty about their economic future.
Here is a document, Mr. Speaker, presented by one of Canada's largest unions, a document that I say might have been drafted by some of our foremost agricultural organizations. In Canada today the farmer and the labourer are coming closer and closer together. The worker realizes that his only chance to obtain a high wage is when the farmer is getting high prices for the commodities he has to sell. Conversely, the only way for the farmer to get high prices for the food products he produces is for the industrial worker to get high wages.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce left me absolutely cold when I heard him say, to the farm implement industry representatives, that wages in the farm implement industry had gone so high that the industry had priced itself out of the market. He said, "I suggest that you find employment elsewhere"-and he described that as being the cold-blooded fact.
I do not think it is a case of high wages pushing up farm machinery prices at all. It is a case of high profits, skyrocketing profits, pushing up farm machinery prices. I would refer the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the brief, at page 5, where it lists increases in profits in the farm implement industry in Canada from 1946 to 1951 and points out that they increased by 223-6 per cent, while the increase in wages during the same period was only 107-1 per cent. The farm implement industry profits far outdistanced the increase in wages of farm implement workers. And if we want employment in the farm implement industry, then the thing to do is not to say to the farm implement workers who are unemployed, "Go to some other place and try to get work somewhere else, so as to bring down the level of wages by competition." That is not the way to solve unemployment in the farm implement industry.
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I say the way to solve unemployment in the farm implement industry is to give our agricultural producers a guarantee that they are going to receive reasonable prices for farm products over the next few years. Assure them that the government is not going to let the bottom drop out of farm prices. If our agricultural industry is given that assurance, then the farmers will buy farm machinery. I have not seen a farmer yet who would prefer to drive a tractor 30 years old, if he could have a new one. I have not yet seen a farmer who prefers to stand out on the side of the road and prime the vacuum tank of an old 1927 Chevrolet truck while one of his neighbours drives by at 50 miles an hour in a 1953 or 1954 model.
All the government has to do, to see that increased purchases are made of farm implements-trucks, automobiles, textiles, and every other thing produced in Canada-is to see that all Canadians have the purchasing power with which to buy those goods. If the government will undertake an adequate system of public works, a program that will stabilize farm income and will improve our social security legislation, it can deal effectively with the unemployment problem, and can at the same time raise the general standard of living of the Canadian people.
I want to point out to hon. members on the government side of the house that such a statement cannot be considered radical. Such a statement cannot be considered irresponsible, since that kind of statement was repeated over and over again by the late prime minister during the war, and immediately thereafter.
The war is now a long distance in the past. The objectives that were held out as the reason for our undertaking such terrible sacrifices apparently have now been forgotten. The great new order we were to see is being heralded in 1954 by half a million unemployed. We are waiting to hear from the government what it intends to do to solve unemployment and to prevent further disaster.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if talk would give employment to people, then we in this chamber would certainly be doing our share to solve the problem in Canada. For two weeks the government has been trying to get into supply. The motion was first moved on February 15. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) then offered an amendment which touched off the present debate on unemployment.
2536	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I am the forty-sixth speaker on the list, and I believe this is the sixth day on which the debate has been proceeding. It must be obvious of course to the people of Canada that members of parliament do view with some seriousness the present unemployment situation. I feel quite sure that all hon. members, whether they be on the government or on the opposition side of the house, do look with a great many misgivings on the present very large number of Canadians who find themselves out of gainful employment.
Continued unemployment on any substantial scale in Canada unquestionably will have an adverse effect on our economy, and will strike fear into the hearts and minds of many people. As a matter of fact, ever since the apparent change in attitude on the part of Russia, and the beginning of the so-called peace talks, there has been a great deal of fear in the minds of our Canadian people. Early last summer the stock market reacted to the possibility that we might be entering a period of peace. During the election campaign last summer the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in a broadcast felt it necessary to reassure the people in this country about this whole matter. He pointed out that Canadians had been enjoying a number of years of prosperity, which he said we had enjoyed in spite of the fact that the government had been obliged to spend no less than two billions of dollars a year on defence. If, he argued at that time, it were possible to maintain prosperity while at the same time spending two billions of dollars a year on defence, then how much greater prosperity could we achieve finally if we got into a period of peace. He said the government then would no longer have to spend two billions of dollars a year on defence and would be able to use that money for the purpose of raising the general level of economic activity and wellbeing in Canada.
I am sure that there is substantial agreement with what the Prime Minister said at that time. I certainly agreed with him; and I do not think anyone in the house would differ. But it seems to me the present large and widespread unemployment in Canada is ample evidence that thus far the Liberal administration has failed in peacetime to keep the economy in a condition of wellbeing. The government minimizes the situation today and makes the claim that we should not be talking about depression. Government members claim that such talk may help to bring on a depression.
Well, of course, I hardly need remind hon. members that in 1929, just before the slump into the depression of the thirties, we were


talking about nothing but boom and prosperity. Then the crash came, and we went into what we now call the dirty thirties, and sometimes the hungry thirties. The government also makes the claim that the prosperity we have been enjoying since 1939 has come as a consequence of Liberal policy. Well, we have enjoyed prosperity since 1939; but it was not because of the virtues of Liberal policy. It has been because the Liberal government has been riding a war-horse for all it is worth. That was how we got into prosperity, the prosperity we have enjoyed since 1939; and that is how we have kept in it.
The government claims that as long as the Liberal party is in office we need not worry about unemployment and its possible consequence, depression, among other things. The government I think is again overoptimistic, because I think that such optimism is dangerous, and especially dangerous if it diverts our attention from the problems that we face.
Then, I want to say something about depression this afternoon, a depression which may result from widespread unemployment. No hon. member, certainly no one who has lived since the late 1920's, needs to be convinced that depression is a fact, and that it can come quickly once it gets started. We know, too, that depressions have occurred from time to time throughout the past as far back almost as anyone can remember. The evidence on this point is overwhelming, and all students of economics accept depressions as an established fact. They also accept that depressions result from policies of men and governments.
In recent years a great amount of statistical work has been done in an attempt to find out whether depressions occur at regular intervals, and if so, what the intervals are. The information that they have gathered together is exceedingly important, and in my judgment very valuable. Nevertheless, the tremendous emphasis which economists and students of economics have placed on what they call the periodicity-that is a big word, I know, and certainly it is not original with me-I say the emphasis that the students of economics have placed upon what they call the periodicity or booms and slumps has had a most unfortunate effect upon thinking. A hundred years ago economists denied the possibility of a general and prolonged depression such as we experienced in the 1930's throughout most of the world. They did not attempt to deny the existence of slumps, however, and consequently argued that a slump is a deflationary movement which lets the hot air

out of a preceding inflationary movement, thus of course restoring the economic balance.
1 say that when undue emphasis is placed upon the periodicity of prosperity and depression it naturally serves to nourish a state of mind in which one expects a slump always to be right on the tail of a boom. That is what they call the boom and bust kind of thinking or philosophy.
It seems easy for those people who do think in terms of the boom and bust sequence to get into the habit of thinking of each upward movement as the cause of the following downward movement, and vice versa, just as one might think of the swing of the pendulum as causing the resultant opposite swing. I think such people, in getting into that habit of thinking, ignore such questions as what set the pendulum swinging in the first place, and what kind of mainspring it is that keeps the pendulum in motion perpetually.
Some economists and others refer to this kind of sequence as a self-generating theory, and they say that our economy is given to this self-generation. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe any such tripe. I do not think it is a theory at all; it is only the standardization of ignorance. Then they try to call it a philosophy. At any rate, the habit of pendulum thinking today is quite widespread. There are those people who are talking as though they are perfectly sure that a depression will inevitably follow the period of postwar prosperity that we have had. Most people have learned a great many things since the boom days of 1929. One of the things we have learned is that no economy could possibly swing back and forth so wildly through one extreme to the other as ours has done without there being something very wrong about it. One outstanding United States economist has said:
There is indeed something very wrong with our economy. It fails to distribute mass consumer purchasing power in sufficient quantity to permit the whole product of industry to be purchased. This failure exists at all times under our system and is bad at all times.
These are the words he used. If our economy were constitutionally sound and well, the expansion which accompanies prosperity would not be unwholesome and dangerous in any way. But, Mr. Speaker, our economy is not sound. The real disease affecting it is a constitutional disease, and we have to look after it in a constitutional manner. In any period of prosperity the flow of mass consumer purchasing power fails to keep pace with the growth of industry. That fact is beginning to become very apparent throughout the whole world.
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
Throughout the 1920's there was a good deal of talk about the discovery by some wise man that high wages paid off in prosperity. Well, it was tried. I can remember the high wages that I earned as a boy; I can also remember some other things that went along with it. The flow of mass consumer purchasing power through increasing wages, however, was expanding throughout practically the whole of the 1920's; but we know now that it was not increasing anything like as fast as the national production. On the contrary, the discrepancy between mass consumer purchasing power and total productive capacity was steadily increasing all the way from 1922 to 1929. At the peak, in the early months of 1929, according to the Brookings Institution's findings, in its very interesting and most illuminating study, "America's Capacity to Produce and Consume", production was 19 per cent short of existing productive capacity. I emphasize that point because it can mean only one thing, namely, that purchasing power is not generated even in peacetime as fast as goods are produced, and that is the serious thing for our consideration.
In spite of the establishment of this fact beyond all successful contradiction, during the past seven or eight years, we have witnessed a constant struggle on the part of labour throughout the country for higher wages, when all the time they would have been infinitely better off if they had been joining in the great drive to try to increase the flow of mass consumer purchasing power, to try to keep up their own purchasing power rather than just to increase the number of dollars that they called take-home pay.
Well, the break came in October, 1929. I will not pause here to try to discuss the steps by which it had come. I think some hon. members have already done that. Let it be enough to say that a few people had already seen that a crash was inevitable, and that it was bound to come sooner or later. They said so. I remember hearing some of them, and for several years depression came and deepened, with production falling off and unemployment of men and dollars steadily increasing, until the winter of 1932-33 in the United States there was an avalanche of bank failures, which brought about real trouble.
In our Canada, right up until 1935, we gradually slumped into the depths of a depression, the like of which we had never experienced in all our days.
At this point the government of the United States-I am speaking of 1933-began a pumppriming action. At first the amount of money
2536	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment they spent was a mere trickle, but the effect of it was felt almost instantaneously. The flow of that money increased continuously, until the winter of 1936 and 1937, when the soldiers' bonus was pyramided on top of the payments made by various recovery agencies, such as W.P.A. and others, when there was a sharp upturn of prosperity in the United States that did have some effect right here in Canada. However, we had not done very much in this country and as a consequence we did not feel the upturn nearly so readily nor so sharply as they did in the United States.
Finally, in 1939, things began to take on a different complexion; but, Mr. Speaker, it was not recovery measures instituted as a consequence of Liberal policies that ended the depression. It was the war. The most bitter critics of the process of government spending our way out of depression are very insistent on this point, that it was the war that brought us out of the depression. All economists recognize that war is a colossal system of public works in a sense. In the course of war industry booms, the volume of production reaches undreamed-of heights, just as it did in Canada. And the whole thing is financed by government funds, much of which is newly created.
Only a comparatively few short months before the outbreak of the war of 1939 the Social Credit group in this house proposed to the Minister of Finance that the government create and spend into circulation in Canada $200 million to get the wheels of industry started again and to provide employment for the unemployed thousands. The Social Credit members at that time were told that they were a bunch of idiots to think of such a thing, that it would bring on the worst kind of inflation, or in the alternative would wreck our economy.
However, it was only a matter of hours after the declaration of war in the fall of 1939 that Mr. Ilsley went to the chartered banks and on his own word arranged with them a substantial expansion of credit amounting to approximately $200 million in order to get the war effort started. Since that time there have been a good many billions of dollars of new purchasing power created and poured into the bloodstream of the economy of Canada. Well, the government continued pouring the mass purchasing power into the economy all during the war and we were able to finance and prosecute a pretty creditable war effort for a small country of 13,500,000 people. And then came peace.
Now in the first year after the war ended, 1946, the governor of the Bank of Canada, reviewing the economic situation in our 

country and the trends of the time, issued a warning in the Bank of Canada report of February 8, 1946. I should like to quote briefly from page 9 where, after reviewing a table showing the national expenditure, Mr. Towers had this to say:
Trends in these components of national expenditure, taken together, will determine whether or not a satisfactory high level of employment and income can be maintained in the years ahead.
Clearly it is the first two items in the expenditure table, comprising total government outlay, which represented the main driving force behind the very high level of activity which was attained during the war period. Canada's problem now is to expand the other types of expenditure, and particularly domestic private investment and domestic consumption, in order that there will be compensating stimulus as government outlays decline to their post-war level.
It is clear that what Mr. Towers foresaw in 1946 was that the government would experience difficulty in maintaining mass consumer purchasing power at a level high enough to stimulate a high level of economic activity. That, he said, would be one of our major problems. On page 10 of the same annual report of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Towers warned the country in these terms:
Looking to the future, however, there is no room for complacency. Most of our real problems of postwar adjustment are still ahead. The backlog of demand will not be large in relation to productive capacity when industry has been fully reconverted and inventories built up to normal levels. When the time lag involved in demobilization is over, government expenditures will fall rapidly. Nor will our foreign lending to finance the purchase of Canadian goods remain indefinitely at the present level. The prevailing optimism on the North American continent is dangerous if it diverts attention from the problems which have to be faced.
Those were sober words and they should have been listened to. They should still be considered as a warning to the Canadian people. It now appears from the size of the unemployment backlog in Canada that the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada have at least gone partly unheeded. We have become complacent and we are now facing a dangerous situation as a consequence. The very fact that the government has not made a pronouncement with respect to the means that they propose to adopt in relation to the unemployment crisis is evidence that we have become complacent.
During wartime Canada built up a huge producing machine which made it possible for us to make, as I said before, a very creditable war effort for a population as small as ours. But efficient as that production machine was during the war, unless care is taken it can cause havoc in peacetime. What we need more than anything else today is a policy, a real down-to-earth policy, for adjusting our nation's purchasing power so that it can match our large

power of production and our still larger possibilities of the immediate future-what we look upon as the atomic future.
Back in the 1930's, when we were in the depths of the depression, we Social Crediters maintained that the government could induce a flow of consumer purchasing power sufficient to absorb the entire product of industry, that is to distribute it, however large the volume of production might be. We contended that there was no economic bar to doing this and that it was only good common horse sense to see that it was done. However, we were laughed at then.
But time has vindicated our contentions. Nobody with any sense or judgment today will deny that the government can induce a flow of consumer purchasing power sufficient to absorb the entire product of industry. People now know that in this respect war is quite like a great system of public works, as I have already said, except that they do not necessarily involve death and destruction.
Government projects are not limited to the production of munitions of war. On the contrary, a public works program in peacetime may produce monuments of enduring value. That is the kind of thing that we believe is possible. The best example is what happened under W.P.A. in the United States during the thirties. The United States government spent many millions of dollars of public funds and in so doing they built schools, hospitals, community halls and all that sort of thing which will stand for many years as monuments to the vision of men who declared that when unemployment begins to show itself the government should induce the flow of consumer purchasing power so as to get things started, and then make use of the purchasing power to build lasting assets that will serve this generation as well as the next and perhaps the next. I point out at once that the United States ran the country into almost hopeless debt unnecessarily in the process of carrying out public works programs.
I think that public works and housing have come almost universally to be accepted as by far the most desirable of governmental recovery measures. Many of the speakers in the present debate have stressed this point and have asked' the government to lose no time in setting up enough works and housing projects so that men who now find themselves out of work will be able to get a job and an income without further delay.
There are so many things that we could be doing. For example, I think we ought to hang our heads in shame as a nation that
1,	1954	2539
Proposed Committee on Unemployment we have grown to 87 years of age and still have not completed a trans-Canada highway. We should have had one a long while ago and it should have been built by the federal government instead of placing so much of the responsibility upon the provincial governments. This is one of the very few countries in the world which have forced the lesser governments to carry a substantial burden of the cost of a trans-nation highway.
The provinces and municipalities are so heavily laden with taxation today and their financial problems are so great that they cannot build the roads which are required if we are to have a trans-Canada highway or a system of highways throughout the country. Mr. Speaker, I think this government should take the lead and not only build the trans-Canada highway but also join with the provinces in the building of a system of secondary highways throughout the whole country. We need great irrigation projects in the west. My friend the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has already mentioned the Red Deer diversion scheme. We have heard a great deal here about the Saskatchewan river project. These projects ought to be built, and when they are built they will stand as lasting monuments to the enterprise of a great people and a forwardlooking government.
I do not intend to weary the house with an interminable list of all the things we need, but I would be remiss in my duty to my own constituency and people if I did not mention the fact that the great Peace river country- that vast inland empire that will be so important to Canada and its strength in the future- needs a railway to the Pacific coast; and while there is a great backlog of unemployed manpower in this country is the time to get started on the building of that road.
I recall with what enthusiasm we looked forward to the post-war period. During the war this very House of Commons appointed what was called the reconstruction committee, if I remember correctly. I think it was under the able chairmanship of the gentleman who has since become Senator Turgeon. That committee studied the economic situation in Canada and the needs of the post-war years most carefully, and came up with a whole bag of suggestions and proposals which the government called its "shelf of projects" for reconstruction. Sometimes I, along with other members of the house, wonder what has happened to that shelf of projects.
I think the Turgeon committee did a good job, and because I think so I am inclined to the belief that what we ought to do now, instead of referring this whole question of unemployment, its causes and cures, to the
2540	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment standing committee on industrial relations, as has been suggested, is to set up a permanent or standing committee o 1 this house. We should charge that committee with the responsibility of a yearly investigation and report to parliament on the facts of unemployment and the general economic situation; and perhaps it should be asked to make recommendations concerning measures that might be taken to keep Canadians busy and the Canadian economy at a high level of activity and wellbeing. This committee might be called the economic research and development committee or some such thing; I do not care what the name might be. If the rules of the house did not limit to one the subamendments that can be moved to a motion of this kind, I would seriously consider moving a subamendment asking for the establishment of such a standing committee.
I am one of those who believe that we should not be spending our time castigating the government and blaming it for every single thing that goes wrong. I believe we all must take our responsibility and so must the taxpayers and the electors of this country.
It has occurred to me that a thoughtful observer who might drop in from some other planet, if he should land on the earth today, would have a hard time understanding our present widespread fear of a coming recession. While he listened to us debating here in this house and forecasting all kinds of gloomy things he would see around this country electronics in great profusion. He would see ingenious gas turbines and all kinds of marvellous new types of machinery and factories. He would see this most awe-inspiring atomic power development just about ready to be used for peacetime purposes. He would not know, nor do we, all the fine things which these resources he sees might bring to Canada. We certainly do not yet know whether working hours will decrease or increase in the future. We know, however, that the output from all our resources, when fully developed, could enrich our people beyond our fondest dreams. Continued increasing prosperity would seem to be the logical result of all the things we have at hand today.
When I think of that I have to ask myself, "What in the world is wrong? Why the fears that we are expressing at this time? Who are the culprits in this whole business of unemployment and of gloom"? I think the real trouble lies in the fact that so far we have all failed to accept our responsibilities in a real effort to gear the nation's income to its powers of production. We should not be too much concerned with placing on the government or on anybody else the blame for the present situation. It


seems to me that we should be concerned with placing the responsibility for leading the country out of it. That is the important thing. Every voter, every member of the business groups, every member of the labour unions, every member of the professional groups as well as every member of this house governs this nation through his action or his lack of action, and particularly by what he demands of his business group, his labour union and his member of parliament. Therefore I say they must take their responsibility.
As a nation we have a tremendous number of mechanical slaves, gadgets that do the dirty work for us and save us all from drudgery and physical exhaustion and the monotony that we would naturally face if we were to do all the work that we used to have to do by hand, and which kept our noses to the grindstone. These things that we have at hand, these mechanical slaves, do not necessarily mean that we can cut working hours to the vanishing point or even near it, nor need they take away from us our jobs. With these gadgets, these machines and factories, we should be making one of the greatest production and distribution efforts the world has ever seen.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that we had figures like the ones I found in a magazine not so long ago. We do not have them, but I wish we had. Perhaps if the kind of standing committee I have suggested were to be set up they could set about gathering such figures and publishing them so our people would know them. I was much interested in figures published in 1950 in a well-known United States publication called Factory Management and Maintenance. This magazine and its editors ventured to set up an estimate of future production in the United States. They pointed out that in 1879,
2.733.000	industrial workers supplied the nation with $109 worth of goods per person. In 1939, 7,887,000 workers gave the people $434 worth of goods per person. On the basis of this trend and having in mind all available information on future mechanization, the editors of this magazine expected
11.140.000	workers in 1950 to supply $637 worth of goods per person. By 1960 it is estimated that out of a population of 150 million, 10,050,000 workers will be available and they will likely produce $717 worth of goods per person. As I say, if a standing committee of the kind I have suggested were set up, we could soon gather a great many interesting facts and figures of this kind for our use in estimating what the future is going to hold for this great country.
I see that my time is rapidly being exhausted, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want

to weary the house any further. But I do suggest in closing that my sympathies are with those who find themselves without work and without incomes. I still have very poignant memories of two years with a job but without income back in the thirties. I went through that experience. Those early thirties were days when many of us were the fattest, healthiest, nakedest people in the world. I am sure that many people suffered far worse than I did, but I went through enough so that my sympathies are with those who find themselves without incomes today. Many of them have bought homes requiring substantial monthly payments. If they cannot pay their mortgage instalments, out they will go and they will lose whatever equities they have in them. A man with no home to go to has really lost his freedom.
We do not need to have a depression, Mr. Speaker, although it is hard to tell the unemployed head of a Canadian family who is being evicted from his home that we are not in one now. I am referring to a real slump. We do not need to have one, and I do not believe we will have one. Our country has a bright future. Our country has plenty to commend it to any enterprising person who wants to live and work here. The greatest blessing that can come to any man in my judgment is to have all the work he can do all the days of his life. We have every cause for optimism, but in our optimism let us not become blind to facts that have such portent for the future.
We do need the kind of watchdog economic committee of this house which I have proposed to be constantly on guard for the Canadian people. I suggest that it be set up immediately to begin its studies. In the meantime the government should meet the present unemployment problem by doing these five particular things, amongst others:
1.	They should increase unemployment insurance benefits and provide for some sort of temporary stay of execution of mortgage foreclosures until economic activity again absorbs the unemployed.
2.	They should press forward with housing plans, with emphasis on low income and low rental schemes. If this is to be effective the interest rates must be brought down, because high interest rates today are the great stumbling block in our housing program.
3.	They should adopt realistic trade policies and conclude trade agreements with all countries willing to trade with us on a mutually satisfactory basis. In particular, Canada should cultivate greater trade with Britain and the sterling area and be prepared to settle balances by accepting some sterling.
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
4.	We should adopt a realistic Canada first policy under which as much as possible of our raw materials will be manufactured in Canada. In particular, we should make absolutely sure that the pipe and other materials that go into the trans-Canada pipe line are as far as possible fabricated in Canada; and we say that any subsidies that are paid, either directly or by way of tax remission, must be paid to Canadian companies and not United States companies. Moreover, in my judgment we must finance development in Canada to a much greater degree than ever before with Canadian capital.
5.	There should be an immediate increase in old age pensions and war veterans allowances. That would provide a greater market for the surpluses of our country and would stimulate greater employment.
I see that my time is used up, and I appreciate the indulgence of the house; but before I sit down may I once more warn all my colleagues in the house against becoming so complacent and optimistic as not to be aware of the portents and signs that face us every day if we just look around.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to repeat the many things that have been said about unemployment already in this debate. However, the situation as it exists in my own riding does bear mentioning. It is serious, and all the fine words from the government benches about the situation improving are not relieving the actual hardship thus far. Further, it seems to me that those occupying the government benches are burying their heads in the sand like the ostrich, hoping that time will pull them out of their dilemma.
The Globe and Mail of February 22 reports the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) as having predicted in Chatham the previous Saturday that there would be a resurgence of employment in March. I am wondering which year he meant. We are into March, 1954, right now, and the only feeling prevalent in my home city of Stratford is one of fear. This feeling of fear is, I think, most pronounced amongst the men laid off at the Canadian National Railways locomotive shops, and their families. This fear also extends to those still employed. There are rumours and fears of further layoffs. The government does nothing to allay those fears.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is further reported to have charged the Progressive Conservative opposition in parliament with sounding "the old Tory cry of blue ruin".
