We can see wonderful prospects for the future. We believe in that ultimate future. But surely we are not preaching blue ruin when we attempt to bring to the attention of the government certain critical conditions as they exist at this moment. This fear I mentioned a moment ago is having drastic results. The merchants of Stratford, while depending on trade with the surrounding rural districts, also depend on trade with people working in Stratford. The reports I receive are that not only the people already laid off are not spending but those still working, and particularly those employed at the C.N.R. shops, fear the future and as a consequence are not spending. This lack of spending naturally brings on the sequel of the merchants not buying and the manufacturers not producing, resulting in the subsequent lay-off of more workers.
I believe it is the government's duty to put these fears at rest. They should take the lead and assure their own employees in the C.N.R. that their jobs are secure. That in itself would give confidence to the country as a whole. In a question I placed on the order paper on February 3 information was sought as to any long-term plans for the full utilization of the locomotive shops in Stratford. The answer was to the effect that while these facilities were excellent for steam locomotive maintenance their use for other railway purposes is limited, but is under study.
Let me bring to the attention of the house the fact that an addition to these shops was completed in October, 1949, at an approximate cost of $500,000. Is it possible the management would be so shortsighted as to spend that kind of money in 1949 and not have some plan for the future? They surely must be able to utilize these premises for some purpose. How about building and repairing freight and passenger equipment?
I have heard it mentioned that gas turbine engines have been considered. If so, could these be developed in Stratford?
A special committee of the Stratford Canadian National Railways federated crafts, representing more than 1,000 mechanical workers, met recently in that city. The following is part of a statement issued by them as reported in the Stratford Beacon-Herald of February 19:
The following modernization has taken place in recent years:
1.	A new annex costing over half a million dollars.
2.	New machinery at an average cost of $400,000 a year over a period of the past eight years.
[Mr. Monteith.l

3.	Modern lighting system.
4.	New boilers and compressor in the power house.
5.	Power supply control system for hydroelectric, and
6.	Heat-treating furnaces.
The Stratford shops are strategically located for the handling of repairs to any type of locomotive in the central region, and the skill and ability _ of shop employees has long been recognized as being of the highest calibre.
It just does not make sense to me to spend millions of dollars on construction and equipment and have no ultimate utilization in mind as dieselization takes place.
The government seem to be most unconcerned about getting rid of the wheat in western Canada. May I say that if they were more concerned about this problem, and also about the export of other agricultural products, we would not be too apprehensive about the immediate future. I can mention cheese factories in my riding that have been closed because of lack of markets. I can tell the house of manufacturing concerns in Perth county that have been accustomed to selling a large percentage of their output in western Canada. Their sales and eventually their employment have dropped precipitously because money is not available in western Canada to purchase these goods. Why does that condition exist? It is because the farmers have wheat instead of money.
I assert, Mr. Speaker, that the present government is manifestly unfair when it seeks to blame a previous Conservative administration for having brought on the depression of 1929 which extended into the thirties. Further, it occurs to me that the government is acting today exactly as it did in 1929, when it ignored obvious signals of economic distress. In that year the late Prime Minister Mackenzie King was in office, and in the house he denied that there was serious unemployment. He later visited Winnipeg and was shocked to be met by a throng of men demanding that he find jobs for them. Surely in 1954 the government might take the lead in alleviating fear, as I think they could well do by establishing a committee to study the situation as it exists today.
Surely such important matters as the loss of stable export markets for the primary products of our farms, our forest, our fisheries and our mines, and the ever-increasing competition both at home and abroad for our secondary industries, warrant the attention of the members of this parliament. It is upon these factors in our economy that a high level of economic activity depends. These problems determine the amount of gainful employment available to our people, because lost markets mean closed factories, lay-offs on our railway systems, and eventually

depressed prices for our farmers because the unemployed worker is unable to buy the things he wants and needs.

Among other factors the minister admitted to the house that keener import competition, increasing competition in world markets, improved technology and accumulation of inventories were all contributing to the situation.
Notwithstanding all that has been said by opposition members, notwithstanding all that has been said by labour delegations which have appeared before parliament during the past three weeks, the government still refuse to admit that the unemployment situation is a serious one. Instead of offering the house and the country some concrete proposals or statement of government policy regarding the unemployment situation, ministers and Liberal members generally are quite content to tell opposition members to keep quiet and wait for the spring.
This seems the only solution the government has offered to the approximately half a million unemployed in this country. Opposition members who attempt to point out the seriousness of the present situation are criticized by government speakers as being propagators of an attitude of gloom. We are assured by the government that once the warm weather arrives the unemployment situation will be alleviated and all will be well. I have on my desk here two memoranda submitted to the cabinet two years ago, one by the city council of Toronto and the other by the municipal council of the township of York. In the interests of our survival as a free people I want to urge the government in all sincerity to grapple with this problem now before it mushrooms into a full-fledged depression. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that by this time the government must realize there are half a million people unemployed in Canada. That has been repeated so often that there is no excuse for ignorance of the matter any longer. It is just a question of the seriousness of the problem that we ought to consider.
Some would go so far as to tell us that this is just a seasonal state of affairs. We even have the British Columbia Times which is printed on the west coast saying that the unemployment situation is strictly seasonal. If our unemployment were found only in lumbering or other industries that might be held up by the weather, then I might be inclined to agree with that statement; but when we read that farm implement workers,

electrical workers, workers in the car and truck industries and textile workers are unemployed, then we know that the statement is incorrect. We know also that those industries should be at the peak of production right now, so there must be something wrong, something that goes much deeper than a seasonal state of affairs.
There have been many suggestions made as to how this problem can be handled. Of course in parliament such as this we retain our own individual opinions, and it is only right that such should be the case. However, as the amendment is worded, there must be two ways in which this problem could be attacked. We must have a long-range plan and we must have immediate assistance.
Whether we have 500,000 unemployed or whether we have 5,000 unemployed, the situation in so far as the person unemployed is concerned is the same. I tell you it is desperate. When a person is unemployed and he knows that his wife and family are depending on him for food, clothing and shelter it becomes pretty serious. The number of people unemployed is not so serious as the fact that we have people unemployed in a country with the wealth and resources about which we boast so loudly; yet nothing is being done.
It will be said that the unemployed can get $24 a week, but how can we expect a man and his family to even exist on that amount? We know there are many workers in cities across this country who could not even pay their rent with $24 a week. You may say that if a person is paying more than that and is unemployed he should cut down on the scale of living to which he has become accustomed. Well, if the condition is seasonal, why should he? Why should that man have to leave his home or the way of life to which he has become used and to which his ordinary employment entitles him? I do not think it is a fair state of affairs. I am going to suggest that that pitiable sum of $24 a week should be increased, and increased right now, to take care of the added cost of living with which our unemployed are faced.
So far as the seasonal end of the matter is concerned, the only way to solve the problem is to see that none of our unemployed go hungry or without the necessities of life, that is without food, clothing and shelter, during the period they are unemployed. At the present time we have over $900 million in the fund, but it is true that even at $24 a week that will not last very long. Regardless of that fact, I think it is up to the government of Canada to see that sufficient money is paid out to our unemployed so they

can at least feel secure that they will be able to supply the bare necessities of life during the period of unemployment.
What is the remedy? I do not think anything would reach into every part of our industrial life quite as much as a speed-up in housing and house construction. Such a course will, I know, affect every industry that is threatening to lay off workmen at the present time, such as the electrical industry, the hardware industry, the lumbering industry, and many of our tradesmen who are out of work. But these things are all going to take time. On all sides of the house we have heard it suggested that we must spend money. Of course this money must come through public spending.
I am now going to refer for a few moments to my own riding of Okanagan-Revelstoke. There are a few things we need there. There are some things that have been hanging fire for some little time. I am going to refer to the public building for the city of Vernon. That building was promised two years ago. Last year $100,000 was voted in order that the construction could be proceeded with, and there is on file with the boards of trade and various interested parties in the city of Vernon correspondence assuring them that the building would be started not this spring or next fall, but that it would be under construction last fall.
Now we note that the estimate for this year has been cut to $25,000. We are told that even yet they have not the plan ready. The building is being held up because they cannot agree on the type of plan or the type of building they are going to erect. That is just one thing that could be speeded up.
I am satisfied that it would certainly meet with the approval of the people of Vernon and district, and that it would assist materially in giving employment to those who are out of work at the present time. That is something that could be started now, and during the summer months of the year it would help to remedy the situation that exists there.
Having regard to the long-range field, I could not help paying close attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones) when he was speaking here a few nights ago and telling of the efforts that had been put forth by the municipal councils in his district. I am well aware of what took place in the city of Kelowna and in surrounding cities. The same thing could be put into operation at the present time. But we are speaking now of the situation as it affects the federal government and federal spending.

It has been gratifying to hear a discussion of the real reasons behind the piling up of inventories, the piling up of goods, namely the lack of purchasing power. In 1951-52 British Columbia's contribution to the national exchequer totalled $239,463,705, an amount which exceeded by $45 million the total collected in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and by more than $150 million the total collections from the four maritime provinces.

With regard to long-range spending, there are various things we should mention. At the present time we hear a little bit of talk about the development of the Columbia basin. This development would solve the power and irrigation problems of a large part of British Columbia. I understand that some work has been done on it. What you might perhaps call the preliminary surveys have been undertaken and the work is under way. But we do not just like that situation, that it is under way. We should like to see a little bit of action, and to feel that this was going to be a matter whose completion we could look forward to at least in our lifetime.
2548	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment Then we speak of highways. British Columbia is an expensive place in which to construct roads. When we see that the total federal allotment for the trans-Canada highway this year is in the neighbourhood of $20 million, we realize that it will not go very far even if British Columbia gets its fair share of that amount. I do not think anybody will dispute the need for this highway in British Columbia. Just to bring the matter home a little bit more, I should like to refer to a clipping I have. I do not like to embarrass the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) in any way, but I was rather amused by a clipping which I cut from the Revelstoke Review a few days ago and which reads as follows:
Many people, particularly in this area, must have been amused last week by the plight of the federal department which shipped a number of motor vehicles by transport to Vancouver by way of the United States from Edmonton.
The big truck was lost for several days. It finally turned up under peculiar circumstances in Seattle.
The point is that even military equipment has to be shipped through a foreign country because Canada doesn't possess an adequate trans-Canada highway, open twelve months of the year.
The Big Bend highway, which has been open for a considerable distance this winter, could easily have been kept open for the whole distance.
That is not a good situation. At the present time we hardly ever refer to the United States as a foreign country. But if that line were closed to us, and the need arose to get military equipment into the north or even into British Columbia, in what way would it get there? It is high time that definite and speedy action was taken to provide a highway into the province not only by way of Big Bend but also by other routes farther north which are just as necessary and should be given consideration.
We have heard a good deal about trade and about the selling of wheat. I get quite a kick out of the campaign of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to get rid of our wheat, but it is a really serious problem to every part of our country. Let me tell you how the trade problem affects British Columbia. Last month we still had two million boxes of apples unsold. I am satisfied that a good many hundred thousand boxes of these apples would have been unloaded in the prairie provinces if the people there had been able to sell their wheat and thus obtain the purchasing power necessary to buy them. I am also satisfied that if all these apples had been sold there would have been a little more money to buy machinery, lack of the sale of which is causing lay-offs in the eastern manufacturing plants.
Our economy is so interwoven that when any part of it is slowed up by a problem every 

other part of the country is affected. Hon. members will say, how are you going to sell the wheat? We know that sales have been restricted through lack of dollars in the sterling areas and the impossibility of converting their sterling into dollars so they can buy. There is a need for all our surplus production, and the suggestion that has been made that the government should take action to speed up trade with the sterling areas certainly should not go unnoticed.
I am rather disappointed that the Minister of Finance has not made a report about what transpired at the conference of commonwealth finance ministers. Possibly we will find out in due time, but I cannot see why we should be kept in ignorance with respect to this very important matter.
Our lumber industry is also affected by the same conditions. A short time ago Mr. Anthony Benn, vice-chairman and joint managing director of Price and Pierce Limited, London, large importers and dealers in lumber, made the following statement in Vancouver, as reported in the British Columbia news letter:
There was no doubt that there was room for greater expansion in trade, but it depended on the assumption that the United Kingdom had dollars to pay for it. This was an ever-present worry, and he felt that it called for twofold action.
Of course he was pleading that we buy British products in order that they in return may be able to buy ours. But an easier solution would be to have an arrangement whereby we would accept their sterling, not necessarily with the idea that we would have to spend it in Britain but with the provision that we could spend it in any part of the commonwealth to buy the things we must import to maintain our present standard of living.
The matter of trade enters into every part of our economy. There is no part of our provinces not affected by the goods that remain unsold despite the fact that they are needed so badly elsewhere. In my own district of Okanagan-Revelstoke the mining industry is also faced with a problem. I was quite concerned a few days ago to receive a letter from the Revelstoke board of trade advising me that they are having a tough time. The letter said that during the past few months at least 300 people have been put out of work as the result of slow-downs and lay-offs in the mines. That is the way it goes. Of course we realize that the low market for base metals is a problem that is going to take a lot of study, but we believe that on the government side of the house there are men who are quite able to give the matter the study it requires. We are satisfied with

their ability, but we are certainly disappointed that they have set up what might correctly be called a curtain of silence with respect to any plans for solving the dilemma with which we are faced at the present time.
I do not believe the opposition should merely sit back and criticize. I think we should be able to offer suggestions once in a while that will perhaps shed a little bit of light or help in some way. Although I should like to commend the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) who brought this problem before the house, I am rather surprised that no real suggestions have been made by the official opposition. After their experience in solving the unemployment problem of the early thirties, one would think they would be able to come forward with plenty of advice.
With respect to the members to my immediate right, I do not know whether or not they have a policy. We hear one man asking that taxes be cut, and we hear another suggesting that the cost of living be reduced. As to the cost of living, I wonder if it would solve the problem if we were able to reduce the cost of living so that the unemployment insurance benefit of $24 a week would provide the necessities of life. In 1930 hamburger was a nickel a pound, but still people did not have the nickel with which to buy it. I do not think that reducing the cost of living is the solution. I do not think that the reduction of taxes is the solution. The only solution is to put into circulation sufficient buying power to maintain the standard of living to which our people have become accustomed and to which they are entitled, and in that way bring back prosperity to our country.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) refer to the shot in the arm administered by the Liberal administration in 1939 when some $200 million was put into circulation for the purpose, as the prime minister of that day said, of solving the unemployment problem, developing our natural resources and speeding up the war effort. If that was a suitable solution for those days, why is it not a solution today? If the government in 1939 was prepared to take measures to solve unemployment and speed up the war effort, why can similar action not be taken today to solve the unemployment problem and speed up the peace effort?

My mental arithmetic indicates this is an increase of 100 per cent. In Prince Edward Island there were 719 receiving benefits in November, 1953, whereas there were only 322 at the end of October, 1952. This is an increase of 125 per cent. In Nova Scotia there were 7,814 receiving benefits this past year, whereas in 1952 the figure stood at 5,100. This shows an increase of 65 per cent, a little lower but nevertheless something to worry about. In New Brunswick, my own province, there were 6,671 receiving benefits as of November, 1953, whereas a year ago there were only 3,853, an increase of 74 per cent.

Everything seems to have been said that could possibly have been said in this debate, yet no subject, I imagine, let alone a subject as important as the unemployment question in Canada today, can be completely covered to the point where nothing remains to be said.
There is one factor, though, that I believe has been overlooked by other speakers who have taken part in this debate, and I should like to take a few minutes to deal with that factor. I believe it has a great bearing on the question of unemployment, and I believe it will continue to aggravate the situation for some time to come.
I am sure all of us in Canada are aware of the fact that a basic cause of unemployment is the position in which agriculture finds itself at the present time. Whenever our agricultural economy is threatened or becomes depressed the inevitable result is that we have a great increase in the number of unemployed in this country. That is especially true in those industries that are dependent on agriculture.
At the moment I should like to quote some facts and figures that would seem to bear out my contention that this is important. One is the fact that over the past few years a great many farms in this country have disappeared. The people who formerly occupied that land have drifted into industries in Canada. As a matter of fact, in 1947 the University of Saskatchewan carried out a survey in that province to ascertain how many people had left the business of farming and gone into other industries. They came up with some very astonishing figures, Mr. Speaker.


In the province of Saskatchewan alone some
43,000	farms had completely disappeared. I do not mean that the land had disappeared, but those farms had been absorbed into other pieces of land to make what are commonly termed economic units. Nevertheless, the fact remains that those 43,000 families left the farms and went into jobs in other industries.
I should like to speak for a moment on some of the reasons for that exodus from the farms to other industries in Canada, and I am sure that what happened in Saskatchewan has happened in a smaller way in a great many other provinces in the Dominion of Canada. Changing economic conditions of course forced these people oil the land. Some people would contend that this was a good thing. These people were farming uneconomic units and therefore were not providing food at the least cost to the consumer. Whether that is true or not, the fact remains that this has happened.
The bulk of these 43,000 farms were composed of quarter sections or less. During the war very little farm machinery was available, with the result that because of the tremendous speeding up of production farmers found at the end of the war that their tools of production were completely worn out. After the war came to an end- I will agree farmers had made considerable money-they were accused of buying machinery and spending a great deal of money unnecessarily. They had to spend this money in order to replace the tools of production that had been completely worn out during the war.
The price of farm machinery rose very rapidly at the close of the war. I am sure a great many hon. members will recall that when the steel companies asked for a 25 per cent rise in the price of steel a great deal of opposition came from this corner of the house, because we realized at that time that if steel were given this increase it would be reflected immediately in the cost of farm machinery. Because of the opposition from this corner of the house the steel companies did not get the 25 per cent increase in the price of steel, but they did manage to get a 12 J per cent increase.
The immediate result was that the cost of farm machinery increased markedly. As the farmers found themselves in the position of having machinery to pay for, the only way in which they could do it was to buy more land and produce more to pay for the machinery. So they went out and bought land, and as a result were able to make their farming operations more economical,

were able to raise more produce at a smaller cost. However, they found that they were not able to sell their production. They were not able to buy more farm machinery because they could not sell the grain they had grown. That was reflected in an unemployment situation in the farm machinery industry, the automotive industry and many other industries related to agriculture in this country. The result is that we have some half million unemployed, a great many of them having been employed in the industries I have mentioned.
This will probably get worse because 50 per cent of the farms remaining in Saskatchewan-and I said a moment ago that you will find this situation existing in other provinces-are still uneconomical. We are going to see another shift from the farms to industry because of that fact. We are going to have another fifty or sixty thousand people displaced from the land who are going to compete with employees in these other industries so far as work is concerned.
A great many things have been said during the course of this debate as to what can be done about a situation such as this. I am sure that an increase in unemployment insurance benefits would greatly help the situation. I think we all realize that is just a stopgap, and that is about all unemployment insurance was intended to be. It was intended to alleviate distress to the point where it would not be too great for the time being.
Mention has been made time and time again during this debate of the fact that we must dispose of our farm surpluses. We must introduce some forward planning into the agriculture industry to allow for the setting of some orderly production goals for farmers. Certainly I do not think the expense of such a plan should fall on the shoulders of the consumer; it should not be set up to do that. We must make a thorough examination of those industries upon which agriculture is dependent for machinery and so on, with a view to eliminating any trace or danger of monopoly or combine operations.
I think without exception every speaker has advocated the making of food available to hungry people. We are sometimes asked who is going to pay for these gifts of food to people in the underdeveloped countries of the world, because there is no doubt they would have to be heavily subsidized by the government. I would say that the people who pay for it should be the same people who are going to be asked to pay for the 50 Bristol Britannia transport aircraft which are to be built by Canadair at a cost of some $185 million to the taxpayers of this country. I say
Proposed Committee on Unemployment that those people should be the people to pay for any subsidization that may be necessary to get food into the hands of people in the underdeveloped areas of the world. It is time we had a closer look at this problem of world hunger and despair.
I am sure that we cannot delay much longer with these issues. We have to make up our minds whether we are going to be part of the cause or part of the cure of world conditions. As Canadians we must accept our responsibility. If we adopt the plan I have mentioned, of getting food into the hands of hungry people throughout the world, certainly it will be said that we were part of the cure rather than part of the cause for the conditions we see in the world today.

It is like the fellow coming home after a big night and telling his wife that he did not spend $584 but spent only $524. There may be half a million more who are on short time. There may be another half a million who are worried about what is going to happen to them. But "Oh, no", the government say, "we do not believe it; it is only seasonal".
Let no one tell you that to point to imminent danger is to do more than point to weakness in our economy. When the government is in business more than any government since confederation, then they should look at the situation. This is the only forum that we especially in the opposition can use. As to hon. members behind this row of cabinet giants and empty seats, the only speeches they make are wisecracks in approval of government policies they do not understand. While the opposition is small, Mr. Speaker, we are about the only group-we here and those to our left-who can express the views of the people. After all, parliament is the forum to which we should bring the grievances of our people.
I am satisfied that there are plenty of grievances, Mr. Speaker. The farmers of Canada are not too well satisfied when they find that over the last two or three years their profits have been falling at least 12 to 15 per cent every year, and that in many lines of products they are now getting half the price they got before. They worry because they see the great unsold surplus of wheat, greater than in any year since confederation. This is the first year in the last

These things concern the labouring men. They concern the people who are undertaking these expensive, extravagant and luxurious construction programs, encouraged by government whispers for fear they will call a halt to their construction. Does that help employment? Does it help employment for the government to tell us to spend less, while at the same time we know they are spending more? It does not help us. Producers are growing nervous because their prices are falling and their taxes are rising. Their costs are higher and their sales are lower. Surely it is not a crime, Mr. Speaker, to bring these facts before parliament even if we have this smug complacency of the government and its supporters, three-quarters of whom are not in the house.

Since I last had the pleasure of speaking on the subamendment the number of unemployed in my own home town of Woodstock, Ontario, has risen from approximately 1,000 to 1,250, and 950 of these are at present drawing unemployment insurance. This, of course, does not include the large proportion of the 2,000 textile workers in the community who are on short time.
The committee suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) should be set up to examine the various factors causing unemployment at the present time. We hope that this committee, if it is set up, will look into the possibility of curing the unemployment situation. I feel there is a very definite necessity for such a committee, and this has been shown increasingly in the speeches delivered in the last day or so of this debate. The principal matter I should like to deal with in the few minutes I shall take is that which was in part referred to by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). On February 16 last, at page 2140 of Hansard, the hon. member had this to say:
If wages continue to increase-and apparently every union is asking for increases-we shall find that we have not only priced ourselves completely out of foreign markets but that we have come to the place where people at home will refuse to buy in the domestic market.
A little further on on the same page he said:
Is it because there is overproduction of radios that they have not radios in those homes? No. The only reason that they have no radios is that they cannot afford to pay the price on the price tag that is hung on the radios.
Still further on the hon. member continued:
Since the question has been asked by the hon. member to my left, I shall do so. I am sorry I did not bring the documents down to my desk. Just a few weeks ago advertisements were sent to me from two papers. One is printed in Windsor, Ontario and the other is printed just across that little bridge in Detroit, Michigan. On the same day two advertisements appeared in the two papers. They are advertisements by the Westinghouse people. They have to do with an automatic washer and dryer. In the United States on that particular day the price was $369.90 and in Windsor it was $689.
The hon. member continued his remarks, but I do not need to read any more. I think they illustrate the point I wish to deal with, namely the high prices of various products in Canada such as appliances, automobiles and automobile accessories. They have become so high in price that people cannot afford to buy them, and since people cannot afford to buy them production of these things has fallen off in Canada and accordingly people are being put out of work.

In this regard, sir, some very interesting remarks were made by one Ira G. Needles, president of B. F. Goodrich Company of Canada. Mr. Needles is a very prominent Canadian industrialist and he made these remarks in Preston, Ontario on February 17 last. I should like to read a brief report of Mr. Needles' remarks which are taken from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of February 18, 1954, as follows:
"Canadian manufacturers are being unjustly criticized for the wide price variance between identical Canadian and United States manufactured goods. The fault rests with the federal government's 10 per cent sales and 15 per cent excise taxes, and the unrealistic practice of applying these taxes at the manufacturing level rather than the retail level."
The article goes on:
He explained that Canadian suggested selling prices must include all taxes, hidden and direct, while most United States prices were tax excluded. The government policy of collecting sales and excise taxes at the manufacturing level results in a retail mark-up being taken on the tax.
"On the popular 6:00-16 tire the tax effect is more than four times the net tax amount in the United States," the speaker said.
Mr. Needles supported his argument with examples of tire prices in both countries. "A 6:00-16 four-ply top quality tire which fits popular car models to 1934 to 1947 sells in Canada at the suggested price of $26.50 including tax. In the United States the same tire is advertised at $20.60, or 22-3 per cent lower.
However, if the sales and excise taxes totalling 25 per cent of the net selling price and the tax effect of the retail mark-up were removed the Canadian tire would sell for $22 as compared to the United States price of $20.60, a difference of only 6-4 per cent," explained Mr. Needles.
That illustrates roughly the effect of excise and sales taxes on products such as appliances, automobile parts and supplies. These taxes have another effect in a purely uneconomic way. They cause a great deal of mistrust and dissension among people in Canada. You hear statements by persons, such as the hon. member for Charlotte, who apparently have not complete knowledge of the situation and who believe that manufacturers are being protected by high tariffs and are taking an unnecessarily high mark-up. You hear questions such as why are prices so much higher in Canada than in the United States; that labour is getting too much and manufacturers are getting too much. This tax, applied at the factory level rather than at the sales level, accounts for much of the difference. The ordinary person is mistaken in his view of the matter, and the result is that labour unions and manufacturers come in for a great deal of unfair criticism. This kind of tax has stirred up a lot of mistrust in the country.
I should like to deal with another matter before I resume my seat. If a committee is
Proposed Committee on Unemployment set up to look into the causes of unemployment and to make suggestions for short-term and long-term remedies, there is one other thing I should like it to consider as well as the sales and excise taxes, namely the question which many of us have heard around the corridors during the last few days. I refer to the question of Canadian companies which are wholly or substantially owned by parent companies in foreign countries, and some of the foreign countries are close at hand. It is said that because of unemployment at home some of the parent companies have been in the habit of taking orders away from Canadian companies.
We have no figures available on this at the moment, but it is a matter that should be studied by the committee if it is set up. If parent companies which have subsidiaries in Canada are taking orders away from Canadian companies, then something should certainly be done about it.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker. In resuming my seat I should like to support the suggestion of the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra that a committee be set up to look into the causes of unemployment and try to find a cure for the present situation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
I do not want to prolong this debate any longer than necessary. Because of the few times I have been on my feet I have not burdened the house for very long, and I do not intend to do so now; but there are a few factors that enter into the employment situation in Canada which have not been emphasized, and I want to mention them, if for no one else's satisfaction at least for my own.
Employment in Canada is dependent upon certain basic realities which we are concerned with. We are employed in Canada because of the kind of country in which we live. I submit that there are four main factors which we should take into consideration as a basis for considering remedies for our unemployment situation. Unless we have a basic approach to the problem we shall neither get a long-term solution nor be able to provide an immediate solution that will stick for any length of time.
Basically we are in this position in Canada. There are four factors that enter into the picture. First of all, the basis of our prosperity is our natural resources. Our standard of living has been built up and our secondary industries have been built upon the exploitation of those natural resources, which in the main are five in number. First is the land; then the fisheries; then the millions of acres of timber area, our trees and our forests; and then the rocks which yield the minerals.
2562	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment Under the rocks in Alberta we have found oil, and we are going to find oil on the prairies. That is the basis of our economy; that is the basis of all employment in Canada.
I am trying to place our employment picture in its proper perspective. I know we can sit down and do homework for five or six or ten hours, or even three or four days, and we can get statistics and gather all the figures. I have statistics piled four feet high up in my office, and if I went through them and had the ability as a parliamentarian I could make a five-hour speech on all the different factors that enter into the economy of Canada.
But that is not the important thing. Sitting down for three or four hours and getting a whole lot of figures and statistics and that sort of thing is not going to lead us to a solution. It is being able to get down to basic facts and using those basic facts as a foundation to do something, to do some high-class figuring and gather the economic factors that enter into prosperity, standards of living, markets, employment and so forth. Then and then only are we going to get anywhere.
We can get all these figures; we have had them for weeks, but they do not mean anything until we get down to the basis upon which our economy depends, upon which our employment depends, upon which our standard of living depends, upon which our exports and markets depend. Natural resources and their exploitation are the basic foundation of the economic development of this country, and provide the basis for all employment. I do not like to talk about unemployment; I like to talk about employment. Let us approach this problem of unemployment from that perspective.
The second factor which enters into this problem in Canada is the climate. We are situated on the northern part of North America. This is the second factor we have to take into consideration. We have rigorous winters. We have spring, then summer, then autumn and then our winter. Some obtuse remarks were made this afternoon about this government or hon. members on this side waiting for the balmy breezes of spring to waft us out of this unemployment era.

speechtext: Some hope.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext: Climate is a very important factor. I put it as the second factor in our employment situation. We have employment in Canada at the times we have because of our climate.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext: The workers have to eat in the winter, too.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
That is right. If my hon. friend has patience I shall come to that. I do want to be brief. The third factor is geography. We talk about trading, the necessity for trade and the influence of world trade upon our employment situation. As I say, geographically Canada is situated on the northern half of the North American continent. On the east we have the Atlantic ocean; on the west we have the Pacific ocean, and to the south of us we have the United States. I have heard a few obtuse remarks pointed at the United States, but after all they are geographically our southern neighbours. Whether we like it or not, they are there. Whether they like it or not, we are here. Our geographical position does affect the flow of our trade-if the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) can restrain his levity-and that has a definite effect upon our markets and our employment situation in Canada.
The fourth and most important of all factors is the brain, brawn and calibre of our people working in harmony with the geographical, climatic and natural endowments which we have in this particular part of the world. If we are to get a long-term solution to our employment problem we must consider these basic factors. Until we appreciate them there is no use talking about palliatives such as increasing unemployment insurance or having the government ask the taxpayers to build dams and public services of one kind and another.
We must realize what constitutes the basis of all employment in Canada, the basis of our prosperity, our standard of living. Our natural resources are the basic reason for having people employed in this country. They have enabled us to create a certain standard of living. We contend as farmers, as workers or as citizens of Canada that we cannot reduce that standard of living. We have got up to a certain level and we want to stay there.
This standard of living has been built up on the factors I have mentioned. In order to preserve that standard of living we must trade with other countries; we just must. There are many things which we cannot produce in this country, which come only from other countries. We talk about the large project at Kitimat, but while we supply the power in order to produce the aluminum we must get the bauxite from somewhere else in the southern hemisphere, and another mineral from somewhere else. They are required in order to produce the aluminum, and thus we enter the international trading phase of the employment situation in Canada.

It is upon that basis only that we can find a permanent solution. It has been pointed out here over and over again that the responsibility rests entirely upon the government and the people who support the government on this side, the ordinary Joes like myself, who have been made to appear as though we do not realize the problem. I do not think there is any group in Canada or anywhere in the world today which recognizes the problem more definitely and more sincerely than we who sit on this side.
Since 1935, because of the policies which have been enunciated from this side of the house, we have been able to widen our markets. As one example, we have sold our wheat in 67 different countries. Within the last few days I had people in my office who came to tell me what the government should do in order to expand markets and international trade. I think this government has been remiss in not telling the people of Canada in a dramatic way that at the present time we have trade representatives who are trying to sell the goods which the people of Canada produce. We have trade representatives in practically every free country of the world. They are knocking at every door.
Just last week I was down to visit this exhibit that is being sent over to Holland. Arrangements are being made for a big trade fair at which Canada will be represented, to show the things the people of Canada make and which we want to sell. That has been going on all the time. The trouble with this government is that it is too modest in publishing its accomplishments. These things are being done all the time.
The people of western Canada were surprised to find that we were selling wheat in 67 different countries of the world. It is true perhaps not so much was sold here as there or some other place, but as the Scots say, many a mickle make a muckle; and if we sell 5 million bushels here and 10 million bushels there, the first thing we know we have got rid of some of our wheat. The same thing holds true all along the line.
I do not care what government you had sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, they could not do more than is being done today. The whole matter of employment is tied up with the international situation. If we look at our papers today, what are the two things that we find emphasized most? We find that those two things are world peace and trade. Those two questions cover the front pages of every newspaper in Canada today. Those are the things upon which the government is working. What do you think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is doing this very night while we
Proposed Committee on Unemployment are sitting here listening to gibes from the opposition? He is on a good-will mission trying to establish human relationships so we can work towards peace which, in its wake, will bring confidence between nations and between peoples. Especially is he trying to establish those human relationships by which the goods that we make in this country can be exchanged for the goods made by people in other countries and which we want, thereby enriching us both.
I am getting just a bit tired, Mr. Speaker- and I know I am not the last to speak-of listening to what we have been hearing. Sometimes it gets a little bit too much under my skin and I speak in spite of myself. As a matter of fact I do not like making speeches, but on the other hand I do not like to have anyone say that we are lacking in appreciation of the difficulties presented by the international and the national situation at the present time. I do not think there is anyone in this house who can take first place in that regard over the people on this side of the house.
If we are going to get anywhere I think we must have-on the part of labour and management, in all sectors and sections of our economic life-discussions between one another. By these discussions we shall be able to arrive at a solution to the employment problem. It will not be easy. You cannot do this overnight. You cannot solve the unemployment problem by having the government act as agent for the taxpayers and hiring all those people who are unemployed.
There is one thing we must remember. I tried to mention it before. The government can spend only what the people whom they govern or for whom they do public business are ready to contribute. If they want to put a great deal more into, shall I say, the kitty, then we can spend a great deal more. There is in existence a public works program running into hundreds of millions of dollars. It will be used only when, in the judgment of the people who are in control of our government, the time is right. That time may come soon.
I just want to come back to this dramatic picture of a lackadaisical government whistling and waiting for the sap to run in the trees when these unemployed people will be back at work. I know that we in western Canada are going to be able to use all the people we can get in the development of the building programs that we have, and so forth. I know these things are not popular to say. It is always difficult to make the ordinary facts of life dramatic. The people in the opposition

It is-I do not know whether I should say it or not; it is nothing personal- the answer to a political prayer, not a personal prayer. No one in the opposition wants to see unemployment. No one wants to see distress; but politically they do.

speechtext:
I might mention something I read in the paper not so long ago. Perhaps I should not say it, but at least I saw it in the paper; I do not know whether or not it is true. One of the members in this house was in Toronto and was advising a certain political organization to see to it that handbills were handed out explaining how this terrible situation in which the people found themselves could be rectified according to the program they had outlined. I have no objection to that procedure. That is all in the deal, but that will not provide a solution.
Without holding up this house for any great length of time, what I am trying to do is emphasize that we in Canada must appreciate the basic facts with regard to our natural resources, our climate, our geography, the quality of brain and brawn of our people and their character, and the financial institutions that we have. We must harness all these, and base our thinking upon these fundamentals. Then we shall come to a long-term solution of unemployment and also be able to decide what immediate steps should be taken.
We are often told that we need a war. I am one of those, Mr. Speaker-and I think I am one of a million-who conscientiously believe that there will not be another war, for the very reason that we are today living in a different age from that in which we used to live. We are living in the Christian era of 1954, but actually we are living in the year 9 of the atomic era. The other era was ushered out with the first atomic bomb that was dropped on Japan. The new era was ushered in with the second atomic bomb that was dropped on Japan. We must now reorientate all our thinking upon the basis of this new era. I hope there will be enough brains, enough sense and enough humani-tarianism among the people who are at the head of our affairs in the world-and I see plenty of signs of it-that we are not going to have another war. This cure that is being brought forward for unemployment, with respect to getting into armaments and so forth, will not, I think, persist. But we are going to bring about a solution to our employment problem, our prosperity problem and our standard of living problem only if we assess all the basic facts and base our


thinking upon them and not so much upon these multitudinous bushels and barrels of figures that are thrown on to the floor of the House of Commons. A solution will be found only if we will get down to brass tacks, assess the world situation, see where we as Canadian people fit into it and then have some high-pressure thinking not only on the part of the government and private members but on the part of trade union leaders, trade union economists, farm organizations, business organizations, and the bankers of Canada; if we get together and discuss it.
This is the era of negotiation. As Dag Hammarskjold said the other day, this is the age of responsibility. Let each sector of the economic life of Canada shoulder its fair share of responsibility. We on this side of the house will take our share. Then we will go forward together to build a greater Canada.
